query.original_query: foundation model epidemic compartmental SIR dynamics representation interpretability time series

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of compartmental epidemic SIR dynamics in foundation models, interpretability of time series forecasting features and circuits for infectious disease modeling
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how foundation models trained on epidemiological time series encode compartmental SIR dynamics within their internal representations. Using sparse autoencoders and activation patching, we analyze the residual stream of a transformer-based forecasting model to identify features that correspond to susceptible, infected, and recovered population states. Our analysis reveals monosemantic features that activate selectively for specific phase transitions, such as the peak infection point or the onset of herd immunity. Causal tracing experiments localize these representations to early MLP layers, where feature steering alters forecast trajectories in a manner consistent with SIR parameter changes. We find that reconstruction fidelity of these sparse features correlates with model accuracy on held-out epidemic curves, while feature splitting occurs when multiple outbreak waves are present. Results show that the model does not rely on a single end-to-end circuit but instead composes separate feature groups for each compartment, with cross-attention heads mediating interactions between infection and recovery dynamics. This work provides a mechanistic interpretability framework for understanding how time series forecasting models internalize known epidemiological laws.

sub_queries.semantic_query: compartmental epidemic models SIR dynamics time series forecasting infectious disease transmission foundation models applied to epidemiological modeling
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the application of foundation models to time series forecasting of infectious disease transmission dynamics, specifically within the framework of compartmental SIR models. Using historical epidemiological data from multiple outbreak settings, we evaluate whether pre-trained deep learning architectures can capture the nonlinear dynamics of susceptible, infected, and recovered populations without explicit mechanistic constraints. We compare forecast accuracy against standard compartmental models fitted via maximum likelihood and ensemble Kalman filtering. Results indicate that foundation models demonstrate competitive short-term predictive performance, particularly during periods of rapid incidence growth, but exhibit systematic biases in long-term forecasts and fail to preserve the structural constraints of the SIR system, such as population conservation. Findings support the hypothesis that while foundation models can approximate observed time series, they do not inherently learn the underlying transmission mechanisms, limiting their utility for counterfactual simulation and policy evaluation. We discuss implications for hybrid modeling approaches that integrate data-driven methods with mechanistic compartmental frameworks.

papers.title: Exploring Representations and Interventions in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how time series foundation models organize knowledge, what interpretable concepts they learn, and how to steer their predictions using conceptual priors.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for analyzing and intervening in time series foundation models, including representation similarity analysis for pruning, concept identification, and steering predictions with conceptual priors.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges representational analysis from language and vision models to TSFMs, offering new methods for building more computationally efficient and transparent time series foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Larger TSFMs exhibit block-like redundancy in representations, which can be leveraged for pruning to improve inference efficiency without significant performance loss.
TSFMs learn intuitive linear concepts (e.g., periodicity, trend) that are localized in specific layers and tokens.
It is possible to steer model predictions by intervening in the latent representations along conceptual directions, enabling concept-informed predictions without additional training.
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) promise to be powerful tools for a wide range of applications. However, their internal representations and learned concepts are still not well understood. In this study, we investigate the structure and redundancy of representations across various TSFMs, examining the self-similarity of model layers within and across different model sizes. This analysis reveals block-like redundancy in the representations, which can be utilized for informed pruning to improve inference speed and efficiency. Additionally, we explore the concepts learned by these models - such as periodicity and trends - and how these can be manipulated through latent space steering to influence model behavior. Our experiments show that steering interventions can introduce new features, e.g., adding periodicity or trends to signals that initially lacked them. These findings underscore the value of representational analysis for optimizing models and demonstrate how conceptual steering offers new possibilities for more controlled and efficient time series analysis with TSFMs.

papers.title: Moirai-MoE: Empowering Time Series Foundation Models with Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.research_question: How can time series foundation models achieve effective unified training by moving from human-imposed frequency-level specialization to automatic token-level specialization using sparse mixture of experts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOIRAI-MOE, a time series foundation model that uses a single input/output projection layer and delegates pattern modeling to sparse mixture of experts, enabling automatic token-level specialization and improving forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: MOIRAI-MOE is an effective approach for time series foundation models, achieving token-level specialization and superior performance in forecasting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
MOIRAI-MOE outperforms existing foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) in both in-distribution and zero-shot forecasting.
The decoder-only training objective is more efficient than the masked encoder approach.
The proposed token clustering gating function outperforms linear projection gating variants.
Model analysis shows that MOIRAI-MOE produces frequency-invariant representations in deeper layers.
Expert allocation reflects time series periodicity patterns, indicating token-level specialization.
future_direction: Pruning underutilized experts for model compression
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models have demonstrated impressive performance as zero-shot forecasters. However, achieving effectively unified training on time series remains an open challenge. Existing approaches introduce some level of model specialization to account for the highly heterogeneous nature of time series data. For instance, Moirai pursues unified training by employing multiple input/output projection layers, each tailored to handle time series at a specific frequency. Similarly, TimesFM maintains a frequency embedding dictionary for this purpose. We identify two major drawbacks to this human-imposed frequency-level model specialization: (1) Frequency is not a reliable indicator of the underlying patterns in time series. For example, time series with different frequencies can display similar patterns, while those with the same frequency may exhibit varied patterns. (2) Non-stationarity is an inherent property of real-world time series, leading to varied distributions even within a short context window of a single time series. Frequency-level specialization is too coarse-grained to capture this level of diversity. To address these limitations, this paper introduces Moirai-MoE, using a single input/output projection layer while delegating the modeling of diverse time series patterns to the sparse mixture of experts (MoE) within Transformers. With these designs, Moirai-MoE reduces reliance on human-defined heuristics and enables automatic token-level specialization. Extensive experiments on 39 datasets demonstrate the superiority of Moirai-MoE over existing foundation models in both in-distribution and zero-shot scenarios. Furthermore, this study conducts comprehensive model analyses to explore the inner workings of time series MoE foundation models and provides valuable insights for future research.

papers.title: On the Internal Semantics of Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do time-series foundation models internally represent fundamental time-series concepts? Specifically, which layers encode which concepts, are concept parameters linearly recoverable, how do representations evolve in terms of disentanglement and abstraction across depth, and how do models process compositions of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic probe-based analysis of time-series foundation models reveals that early layers capture local, time-domain patterns while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, and that while atomic concepts are linearly recoverable, representing compositions of concepts remains a challenge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a structured account of TSFM semantics, showing a layered hierarchy of concept learning and highlighting composition as a key limitation for representing interacting temporal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns such as AR(1) coefficient, trend slope, and level shifts.
Deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals (e.g., variance shifts), with representations becoming more disentangled and abstract with depth.
Spectral and time-warping concepts are the least linearly recoverable from model embeddings.
TSFMs exhibit strong linear compositional properties for most concept pairs, but probe performance degrades for composite concepts, revealing interference.
Representations become more organized and linearly recoverable with increased context length in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
While atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs’ ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.
Spectral and time-warping factors are the least linearly accessible.
future_direction: Explore additional TSFMs, multivariate and irregular datasets.
Adopt controlled-capacity non-linear or causal probes.
Investigate architectures and objectives that better linearize phase and time-warping, and non-linear conditional steering.
papers.abstract: Time-series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as a universal paradigm for learning across diverse temporal domains. However, despite their empirical success, the internal mechanisms by which these models represent fundamental time-series concepts remain poorly understood. In this work, we undertake a systematic investigation of concept interpretability in TSFMs. Specifically, we examine: (i) which layers encode which concepts, (ii) whether concept parameters are linearly recoverable, (iii) how representations evolve in terms of concept disentanglement and abstraction across model depth, and (iv) how models process compositions of concepts. We systematically probe these questions using layer-wise analyses, linear recoverability tests, and representation similarity measures, providing a structured account of TSFM semantics. The resulting insights show that early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns (e.g., AR(1), level shifts, trends), while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, with spectral and warping factors remaining the hardest to recover linearly. In compositional settings, however, probe performance degrades, revealing interference between concepts. This highlights that while atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs' ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.

papers.title: time2time: Causal Intervention in Hidden States to Simulate Rare Events in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do time series foundation models internalize semantic concepts like market regimes, and can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare events such as market crashes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation transplantation, a causal intervention method that provides evidence that time series foundation models learn high-level semantic concepts of real-world events, enabling steerable simulations for stress-testing.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides causal evidence that time series foundation models encode abstract, steerable market regime concepts, enabling deterministic control of forecasts and revealing a continuous severity axis in their latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Activation transplantation can deterministically steer forecasts by implanting the statistical signature of one event into another.
Models encode event severity as a continuous latent variable, with the activation vector norm correlating with shock magnitude.
The steerable representations are robust across different model architectures (decoder-only Toto and encoder-decoder Chronos).
A unified 'crash' concept emerges across layers, with early layers showing anti-correlation and later layers converging to a shared subspace.
The model's internal representation of a crash is not binary but continuous, allowing for graded interventions.
papers.limitation: The work is a foundational proof-of-concept and it remains to be investigated whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal beyond Transformers to other architectures like State Space Models or LSTMs.
future_direction: Investigate whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal across sequence models beyond Transformers, such as State Space Models and LSTMs.
Discover a broader semantic vocabulary within TSFMs, probing for concepts like earnings surprises in finance or seizure onsets in EEG data.
papers.abstract: While transformer-based foundation models excel at forecasting routine patterns, two questions remain: do they internalize semantic concepts such as market regimes, or merely fit curves? And can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare, high-stakes events such as market crashes? To investigate this, we introduce activation transplantation, a causal intervention that manipulates hidden states by imposing the statistical moments of one event (e.g., a historical crash) onto another (e.g., a calm period) during the forward pass. This procedure deterministically steers forecasts: injecting crash semantics induces downturn predictions, while injecting calm semantics suppresses crashes and restores stability. Beyond binary control, we find that models encode a graded notion of event severity, with the latent vector norm directly correlating with the magnitude of systemic shocks. Validated across two architecturally distinct TSFMs, Toto (decoder only) and Chronos (encoder-decoder), our results demonstrate that steerable, semantically grounded representations are a robust property of large time series transformers. Our findings provide evidence for a latent concept space that governs model predictions, shifting interpretability from post-hoc attribution to direct causal intervention, and enabling semantic "what-if" analysis for strategic stress-testing.

papers.title: Benchmarking Attention-Based Interpretability of Deep Learning in Multivariate Time Series Predictions
papers.research_question: How well do attention-based deep learning models perform in terms of prediction accuracy and interpretability correctness on multivariate time series forecasting tasks, and can they correctly identify underlying causal relationships in synthetic datasets?
papers.core_contribution: This paper designs a novel benchmark of synthetic datasets with transparent underlying generating processes to evaluate attention-based deep learning models for multivariate time series forecasting. It finds that while most models have satisfying prediction performance, they often fail to provide correct interpretability, with IMV-LSTM being the only model that achieves both good prediction and correct interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that attention-based models often learn to predict without understanding the underlying data generating process, and only IMV-LSTM provides correct interpretability for most datasets. The benchmark highlights the need for more stable and faithful interpretability in neural architectures for time series.
papers.key_findings:
Most attention-based models (seq2graph, TCDF, DA-RNN) fail to provide correct interpretability of the underlying data generating process, even when prediction performance is good.
IMV-LSTM is the only model that provides both satisfying prediction performance and correct interpretability for most synthetic datasets.
Interpretability correctness of IMV-LSTM increases with dataset complexity, as seen in statistical and mechanistic models (Ising model and Logistic map).
Models like seq2graph show low confidence in their interpretability, with attention weights often biased and having high variance.
TCDF model can correctly identify causality when it does, but it fails to do so consistently across experiments and datasets.
papers.limitation: The experimental settings are mainly focused on multivariate time series single output forecasting tasks and specific well-known generative processes, which may not cover all real-world domains.
future_direction: Extend experimental settings to other multivariate prediction tasks, including multi-input/multi-output classification and forecasting settings.
Incorporate real-world datasets from various domains into the benchmark.
papers.abstract: The adaptation of deep learning models within safety-critical systems cannot rely only on good prediction performance but needs to provide interpretable and robust explanations for their decisions. When modeling complex sequences, attention mechanisms are regarded as the established approach to support deep neural networks with intrinsic interpretability. This paper focuses on the emerging trend of specifically designing diagnostic datasets for understanding the inner workings of attention mechanism based deep learning models for multivariate forecasting tasks. We design a novel benchmark of synthetically designed datasets with the transparent underlying generating process of multiple time series interactions with increasing complexity. The benchmark enables empirical evaluation of the performance of attention based deep neural networks in three different aspects: (i) prediction performance score, (ii) interpretability correctness, (iii) sensitivity analysis. Our analysis shows that although most models have satisfying and stable prediction performance results, they often fail to give correct interpretability. The only model with both a satisfying performance score and correct interpretability is IMV-LSTM, capturing both autocorrelations and crosscorrelations between multiple time series. Interestingly, while evaluating IMV-LSTM on simulated data from statistical and mechanistic models, the correctness of interpretability increases with more complex datasets.

papers.title: Interpretability for Time Series Transformers using A Concept Bottleneck Framework
papers.research_question: How can we make time series transformers interpretable by steering them to learn predefined, interpretable concepts while maintaining forecasting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models and Centered Kernel Alignment to steer time series transformers to learn predefined interpretable concepts (e.g., a linear surrogate model and time features) in a designated bottleneck layer, improving interpretability without significantly harming forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: The concept bottleneck framework successfully improves the interpretability of time series transformers by encouraging specific components to align with human-understandable concepts, with minimal impact on forecasting accuracy, and enables faithful local interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework maintains model performance (MSE, MAE) on benchmark datasets while making the bottleneck layer's representations highly similar to the predefined concepts, as measured by CKA.
Component visualizations and activation patching interventions confirm that the bottleneck components learn and causally influence the model's predictions based on the intended concepts.
The framework is successfully applied to three different transformer architectures (Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer, FEDformer) on synthetic and real-world time series data.
Including a 'free' component in the bottleneck (not constrained by concepts) can help maintain performance and capture additional, non-predefined patterns in the data.
The intervention experiment demonstrates that the model's performance on time-shifted data can be restored by patching the activations of the time-concept component, confirming the causal role of the bottleneck.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes that relevant, interpretable concepts are known a priori and provided to the model.
The framework introduces additional computational cost during training due to the CKA loss calculation.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of sequential data beyond time series.
Exploring more complex or domain-specific interpretable concepts.
Investigating the use of the framework for model debugging and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability focuses on reverse engineering the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. We extend our focus and propose to mechanistically forward engineer using our framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models. In the context of long-term time series forecasting, we modify the training objective to encourage a model to develop representations which are similar to predefined, interpretable concepts using Centered Kernel Alignment. This steers the bottleneck components to learn the predefined concepts, while allowing other components to learn other, undefined concepts. We apply the framework to the Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer and FEDformer, and present an in-depth analysis on synthetic data and on a variety of benchmark datasets. We find that the model performance remains mostly unaffected, while the model shows much improved interpretability. Additionally, we verify the interpretation of the bottleneck components with an intervention experiment using activation patching.

papers.title: Interpretable Additive Recurrent Neural Networks For Multivariate Clinical Time Series
papers.research_question: How to build accurate time series models that are interpretable, specifically for clinical time series data, allowing users to understand the contribution of individual input features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Interpretable-RNN (I-RNN), an additive recurrent neural network model for clinical time series that provides interpretable feature contributions (global and local feature importances) while achieving accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art black-box models.
papers.conclusion: The I-RNN model provides an interpretable and accurate approach for clinical time series prediction, enabling trust and validation in healthcare applications without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
I-RNN achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art RNN models (GRU-D, RITS) on hemodynamic intervention prediction (AUC ~0.86) and similar performance on in-hospital mortality prediction.
I-RNN provides interpretable risk curves and feature importances directly from its hidden state activations, which correlate with input features and the prediction target.
The model refutes the common tradeoff between accuracy and interpretability in time series modeling for clinical data.
I-RNN does not use missingness information as input, which may improve generalization across different clinical practice patterns compared to models that exploit informative missingness.
The additive structure of I-RNN allows for easy validation and correction of feature-outcome associations by domain experts.
papers.limitation: The model may not generalize well to institutions with different care patterns because it does not use missingness information, which can be informative but also institution-specific.
papers.abstract: Time series models with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can have high accuracy but are unfortunately difficult to interpret as a result of feature-interactions, temporal-interactions, and non-linear transformations. Interpretability is important in domains like healthcare where constructing models that provide insight into the relationships they have learned are required to validate and trust model predictions. We want accurate time series models where users can understand the contribution of individual input features. We present the Interpretable-RNN (I-RNN) that balances model complexity and accuracy by forcing the relationship between variables in the model to be additive. Interactions are restricted between hidden states of the RNN and additively combined at the final step. I-RNN specifically captures the unique characteristics of clinical time series, which are unevenly sampled in time, asynchronously acquired, and have missing data. Importantly, the hidden state activations represent feature coefficients that correlate with the prediction target and can be visualized as risk curves that capture the global relationship between individual input features and the outcome. We evaluate the I-RNN model on the Physionet 2012 Challenge dataset to predict in-hospital mortality, and on a real-world clinical decision support task: predicting hemodynamic interventions in the intensive care unit. I-RNN provides explanations in the form of global and local feature importances comparable to highly intelligible models like decision trees trained on hand-engineered features while significantly outperforming them. I-RNN remains intelligible while providing accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art decay-based and interpolation-based recurrent time series models. The experimental results on real-world clinical datasets refute the myth that there is a tradeoff between accuracy and interpretability.

papers.title: EDformer: Embedded Decomposition Transformer for Interpretable Multivariate Time Series Predictions
papers.research_question: This paper addresses the challenge of long-term forecasting for multivariate time series, using historical data.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EDformer, a transformer-based model for multivariate time series forecasting that uses decomposition and reverse embedding to capture seasonal and trend components, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: EDformer is a novel transformer-based model that integrates decomposition and reverse embedding, achieving state-of-the-art forecasting performance and efficiency, while also providing interpretability through feature importance analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EDformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple long-term and short-term forecasting benchmarks.
The decomposition and reverse embedding components are essential for performance, as shown in ablation studies.
EDformer is computationally efficient, with faster training and inference times compared to other models.
Explainability analysis shows that EDformer benefits most from feature importance methods, indicating robust feature utilization.
The model performs well on both high-dimensional and low-dimensional time series data.
future_direction: Test the model on real-life time series datasets.
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is a crucial challenge with significant applications in areas such as weather prediction, stock market analysis, and scientific simulations. This paper introduces an embedded decomposed transformer, 'EDformer', for multivariate time series forecasting tasks. Without altering the fundamental elements, we reuse the Transformer architecture and consider the capable functions of its constituent parts in this work. Edformer first decomposes the input multivariate signal into seasonal and trend components. Next, the prominent multivariate seasonal component is reconstructed across the reverse dimensions, followed by applying the attention mechanism and feed-forward network in the encoder stage. In particular, the feed-forward network is used for each variable frame to learn nonlinear representations, while the attention mechanism uses the time points of individual seasonal series embedded within variate frames to capture multivariate correlations. Therefore, the trend signal is added with projection and performs the final forecasting. The EDformer model obtains state-of-the-art predicting results in terms of accuracy and efficiency on complex real-world time series datasets. This paper also addresses model explainability techniques to provide insights into how the model makes its predictions and why specific features or time steps are important, enhancing the interpretability and trustworthiness of the forecasting results.

papers.title: SOM-VAE: Interpretable Discrete Representation Learning on Time Series
papers.research_question: How to learn interpretable discrete representations of time series that are smooth and provide superior clustering performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SOM-VAE, a framework for learning interpretable discrete representations of time series, featuring a gradient-based self-organizing map and an integrated Markov model for temporal smoothness and improved clustering.
papers.conclusion: SOM-VAE can recover topologically interpretable state representations on time series and static data, improves clustering performance over standard methods, and offers interpretable visualizations that could aid in domains like healthcare.
papers.key_findings:
SOM-VAE outperforms baselines like k-means, VQ-VAE, and traditional SOM in clustering performance on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST in terms of purity and NMI.
The gradient-based SOM training (GB-SOM) performs better than the original SOM algorithm.
The probabilistic Markov model can be learned concurrently with the SOM-VAE and improves clustering performance on noisy data, such as medical time series.
On the chaotic Lorenz system, SOM-VAE learns interpretable representations that capture the macro-states (attractor basins) while ignoring chaotic noise.
On real medical data from the eICU database, SOM-VAE-prob learns representations that are informative for downstream prediction tasks and provides interpretable visualizations of patient trajectories.
future_direction: Extend the probabilistic component for predictions using higher-order Markov Models, Hidden Markov Models, or Gaussian Processes.
Find more theoretically principled ways to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning.
Learn the neighborhood structure as a graph directly from data instead of fixing a latent space structure like a 2D grid.
papers.abstract: High-dimensional time series are common in many domains. Since human cognition is not optimized to work well in high-dimensional spaces, these areas could benefit from interpretable low-dimensional representations. However, most representation learning algorithms for time series data are difficult to interpret. This is due to non-intuitive mappings from data features to salient properties of the representation and non-smoothness over time. To address this problem, we propose a new representation learning framework building on ideas from interpretable discrete dimensionality reduction and deep generative modeling. This framework allows us to learn discrete representations of time series, which give rise to smooth and interpretable embeddings with superior clustering performance. We introduce a new way to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning and present a gradient-based version of the traditional self-organizing map algorithm that is more performant than the original. Furthermore, to allow for a probabilistic interpretation of our method, we integrate a Markov model in the representation space. This model uncovers the temporal transition structure, improves clustering performance even further and provides additional explanatory insights as well as a natural representation of uncertainty. We evaluate our model in terms of clustering performance and interpretability on static (Fashion-)MNIST data, a time series of linearly interpolated (Fashion-)MNIST images, a chaotic Lorenz attractor system with two macro states, as well as on a challenging real world medical time series application on the eICU data set. Our learned representations compare favorably with competitor methods and facilitate downstream tasks on the real world data.

papers.title: The Few Govern the Many:Unveiling Few-Layer Dominance for Time Series Models
papers.research_question: Why do larger time series models not always perform better (scaling paradox), and what is the root cause?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a scaling paradox in time series models where larger models do not perform better, discovers that only a few layers are functionally important (few-layer dominance), and proposes a pruning method to retain these critical layers, achieving comparable or better performance with fewer parameters and faster inference.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that few-layer dominance is a key phenomenon in time series models, and pruning redundant layers can lead to efficient and high-performing models.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling paradox is pervasive in time series models: larger models do not necessarily achieve better performance.
The root cause is few-layer dominance: only a small subset of layers are functionally important, while others are redundant.
Retaining only the critical layers (e.g., 21% of parameters) can achieve superior performance, faster inference, and up to 12% accuracy improvement.
The pruning method is universal and works on 8 SOTA models, retaining less than 30% of layers achieves comparable or superior accuracy in over 95% of tasks.
Increasing data volume or diversity does not alleviate the scaling paradox.
future_direction: Incorporate few-layer dominance into architectural design of large-scale time series models.
papers.abstract: Large-scale models are at the forefront of time series (TS) forecasting, dominated by two paradigms: fine-tuning text-based Large Language Models (LLM4TS) and training Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) from scratch. Both approaches share a foundational assumption that scaling up model capacity and data volume leads to improved performance. However, we observe a \textit{\textbf{scaling paradox}} in TS models, revealing a puzzling phenomenon that larger models do \emph{NOT} achieve better performance. Through extensive experiments on two model families across four scales (100M to 1.7B parameters) and diverse data (up to 6B observations), we rigorously confirm that the scaling paradox is a pervasive issue. We then diagnose its root cause by analyzing internal representations, identifying a phenomenon we call \textit{few-layer dominance}: only a small subset of layers are functionally important, while the majority are redundant, under-utilized, and can even distract training. Based on this discovery, we propose a practical method to automatically identify and retain only these dominant layers. In our models, retaining only 21\% of the parameters achieves up to a 12\% accuracy improvement and a 2.7$\times$ inference speedup. We validate the universality of our method on 8 prominent SOTA models (LLM4TS and TSFMs, 90M to 6B), showing that retaining less than 30\% of layers achieves comparable or superior accuracy in over 95\% of tasks.

papers.title: Causal-oriented representation learning for time-series forecasting based on the spatiotemporal information transformation
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis and multistep forecasting be jointly performed from a unified perspective to understand system dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), a neural network framework that jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective.
papers.conclusion: CReP effectively achieves multi-step-ahead forecasting and infers causal networks for target variables, offering a comprehensive understanding of system dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
CReP demonstrates satisfactory forecasting performance with low RMSE and high PCC on simulation models like Lorenz 96.
The framework successfully infers cause and effect networks for target variables, aligning with known causal structures.
CReP applies to real-world datasets, such as cardiovascular inpatients and COVID-19 spread, providing practical insights.
Ablation studies show that all loss components (reconstruction, future-consistency, orthogonal) are necessary for optimal performance.
The method is self-supervised and handles nonlinearity and non-separability better than Granger causality-based approaches.
papers.abstract: In real-world high-dimensional systems, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. However, effective approaches to synthesize these two interconnected aspects for deeper insights remain lacking. Here we show a neural network framework, the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), which jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective. CReP implicitly learns latent causal representations from observed data while simultaneously making multistep predictions, and explicitly interprets the representations to uncover the causes and effects of target variable. The core idea of CReP is to decompose the original space into three orthogonal latent factors, each capturing distinct causal representations: cause-related, effect-related, and non-causal representations of the target variable. The reconstruction-based dynamic causation, generalized through spatiotemporal information (STI) transformation mechanism, provides a theoretical foundation for simultaneously modeling causal interactions via latent representations and predicting future states using the effect representation. Evaluations on three simulation models and two real-world datasets demonstrate CReP’s robust forecasting accuracy and reliable causal insights. As a self-supervised-learning approach, CReP shows significant potential for practical applications and provides a unified framework to reveal intrinsic mechanisms in dynamical systems by integrating causal relationships and temporal information. In complex high-dimensional systems like power grids or COVID-19 transmission, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. This paper presents Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor, a neural network framework designed to jointly conduct causal analysis and multistep forecasting.

papers.title: Sequential pattern transformer (SPT): a generative and interpretable framework for predicting disease trajectories
papers.research_question: How can we develop a model that goes beyond simple prediction to generate explainable disease trajectories, addressing noise in electronic health records and lack of interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Sequential Pattern Transformer (SPT), a framework that integrates sequential pattern mining with a generative transformer to predict and generate explainable disease trajectories, addressing noise and interpretability in clinical data.
papers.conclusion: SPT provides a transparent, robust, and scalable framework for mapping the complex temporal dynamics of disease, bridging the gap between high-performance AI and interpretable clinical application.
papers.key_findings:
SPT achieved 85.78% Top-5 accuracy, significantly outperforming an LSTM baseline (71.47%).
The model generates clinically coherent disease trajectories, with stable BLEU-1 and ROUGE-L scores over generation horizons.
Interpretability analysis reveals learned disease relationships that align with clinical knowledge, such as clustering of cardiorenal metabolic conditions.
Model performance improves with longer patient histories, indicating effective use of contextual information for prediction.
The framework is domain-agnostic and capable of efficient fine-tuning for adaptation to diverse clinical conditions.
papers.limitation:
Dataset is inpatient-only, providing deep insight into acute exacerbations but lacking the long-term outpatient history of chronic illness.
Methodology concentrates on common disease trajectories and is not intended for rare diseases or highly atypical patient journeys.
future_direction: Incorporate outpatient data to create a more holistic model of disease progression.
Enhance the framework with time-aware attention mechanisms to explicitly model intervals between clinical events.
Assess the framework's real-world value through prospective clinical trials to determine impact on patient outcomes.
papers.abstract: Abstract The effective integration of artificial intelligence into clinical workflows requires models that go beyond simple prediction to generate comprehensive, explainable, and actionable disease trajectories. Addressing the limitations of opaque deep learning architectures and the noise inherent in electronic health records, we introduce the sequential pattern transformer (SPT), a novel framework that synergizes sequential pattern mining with generative transformer modeling. Using four years of inpatient data from 258,460 type 2 diabetes patients, we applied the PrefixSpan algorithm to distill noisy diagnostic histories into a curated vocabulary of 95,630 statistically validated disease progression patterns. A decoder-only transformer was trained exclusively on these evidence-based sequences to learn the temporal dynamics of disease evolution. This pattern-guided approach shifts the modeling paradigm from classification to probabilistic trajectory generation. The model achieved a robust 85.78% Top-5 accuracy, significantly outperforming a standard LSTM baseline (71.47%). Beyond predictive accuracy, the framework constructs a dynamic Disease Atlas, a branching tree structure that visualizes likely future pathways, augmented by multi-level explainable AI (XAI) including learned clinical clusters, SHAP-based feature attribution, and counterfactual simulations. Crucially, this methodology is domain-agnostic and capable of efficient fine-tuning, making it a transferable solution for adapting to diverse clinical conditions and local hospital settings. SPT thus offers a transparent, robust, and scalable framework for mapping the complex temporal dynamics of disease, bridging the gap between high-performance AI and interpretable clinical application.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-based Time Series Classification
papers.research_question: What novel insights can Mechanistic Interpretability methods, specifically, activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, yield when adapted to Time Series Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders to Time Series Transformers, enabling causal probing at the layer, head, and timestep levels, and constructs directed causal graphs to map information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Mechanistic Interpretability techniques can be meaningfully adapted to Time Series Transformers, revealing causal circuits and latent features that enhance understanding of model internals for time series classification.
papers.key_findings:
Patching early layers (Layer 0) yields the largest increase in true-class probability, indicating strong causal signal at the model's entry point.
Individual attention heads (e.g., Head 6 in Layer 0) have significant causal influence, with patching raising true-class confidence substantially.
Specific timesteps are critical for correct classification, and their effects are non-additive due to nonlinear interactions within the model.
Attention saliency provides observational insights into which timesteps heads attend to, but does not imply causation.
Sparse autoencoders can uncover class-specific temporal motifs, suggesting disentangled latent features in the model's internal representations.
papers.limitation:
MI methods remain labor-intensive, requiring substantial domain expertise for pair selection, granularity choices, and interpretation.
The patching experiments focus solely on attention heads, leaving other components like MLP blocks, residual streams, and embeddings unexplored.
Time series features lack clear semantics compared to NLP tokens, making interpretation of causal motifs inherently more challenging.
Interventions can interfere or synergize non-additively due to the transformer's complex interplay of components, complicating isolation of independent causal factors.
future_direction: Expanding patching to include MLP activations, residual streams, and embeddings for a more comprehensive view.
Scaling analysis to multiple clean–corrupt pairs across classes and datasets to test generality of discovered circuits.
Integrating optimization-driven search to automatically identify minimal, non-redundant patch sets for causal graph construction.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have become state-of-the-art tools in various machine learning tasks, including time series classification, yet their complexity makes understanding their internal decision-making challenging. Existing explainability methods often focus on input-output attributions, leaving the internal mechanisms largely opaque. This paper addresses this gap by adapting various Mechanistic Interpretability techniques; activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, from NLP to transformer architectures designed explicitly for time series classification. We systematically probe the internal causal roles of individual attention heads and timesteps, revealing causal structures within these models. Through experimentation on a benchmark time series dataset, we construct causal graphs illustrating how information propagates internally, highlighting key attention heads and temporal positions driving correct classifications. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders for uncovering interpretable latent features. Our findings provide both methodological contributions to transformer interpretability and novel insights into the functional mechanics underlying transformer performance in time series classification tasks.

papers.title: Towards mechanistic understanding in a data-driven weather model: internal activations reveal interpretable physical features
papers.research_question: Whether interpretable abstractions corresponding to physical features are present in the internal representations of data-driven physics models like GraphCast, and if these abstractions are physically consistent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable physical features from the internal activations of the data-driven weather model GraphCast, and that modifying these features leads to physically consistent changes in predictions, offering a window into the model's black-box behavior.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders applied to GraphCast extract highly interpretable physical features, and modifying these features allows probing of the model's internal abstractions, contributing to model trust and potential scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features in GraphCast corresponding to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal/seasonal patterns, precipitation, geographical coding, and sea-ice extent.
Features like sea-ice extent are learned dynamically even though not present in the model's input or output.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are identified, reflecting potential architecture bias.
Sparse probing identifies single features that strongly predict tropical cyclones and atmospheric rivers.
Interventions that modify a tropical cyclone feature lead to interpretable and physically consistent changes in hurricane strength and evolution in the model's predictions.
papers.limitation:
The correlation between sea-ice features and actual ice extent is demonstrated, but a more rigorous causal analysis is needed for a complete account.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are spurious and potentially undesirable from an interpretability perspective.
ERA5 fields themselves are not in perfect hydrostatic balance, which affects the evaluation of physical consistency.
future_direction: Conduct more rigorous causal analysis of the discovered features.
Build mechanistic accounts for the interaction of features leading to model predictions.
Train specifically sparse models to have interpretable computations.
papers.abstract: Large data-driven physics models like DeepMind's weather model GraphCast have empirically succeeded in parameterizing time operators for complex dynamical systems with an accuracy reaching or in some cases exceeding that of traditional physics-based solvers. Unfortunately, how these data-driven models perform computations is largely unknown and whether their internal representations are interpretable or physically consistent is an open question. Here, we adapt tools from interpretability research in Large Language Models to analyze intermediate computational layers in GraphCast, leveraging sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable features in the neuron space of the model. We uncover distinct features on a wide range of length and time scales that correspond to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal and seasonal behavior, large-scale precipitation patterns, specific geographical coding, and sea-ice extent, among others. We further demonstrate how the precise abstraction of these features can be probed via interventions on the prediction steps of the model. As a case study, we sparsely modify a feature corresponding to tropical cyclones in GraphCast and observe interpretable and physically consistent modifications to evolving hurricanes. Such methods offer a window into the black-box behavior of data-driven physics models and are a step towards realizing their potential as trustworthy predictors and scientifically valuable tools for discovery.

papers.title: Finding the DeepDream for Time Series: Activation Maximization for Univariate Time Series
papers.research_question: How can activation maximization be adapted to time series data to improve model interpretability and generate realistic, informative sequences?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sequence Dreaming, an adaptation of Activation Maximization for univariate time series, enhanced with regularization techniques to generate realistic and interpretable sequences that reveal salient temporal features learned by neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Sequence Dreaming, with enhanced regularization, effectively generates activation-maximizing time series for interpretability, allowing precise targeting of activation regions and providing insights into the model's internal processes.
papers.key_findings:
Sequence Dreaming can generate time series that target specific activation regions (e.g., class centers or borders) in the model's activation space.
The method produces smoother and more realistic time series compared to other activation maximization approaches, as validated by visual and quantitative (Mahalanobis distance) evaluation.
The generated time series are often out-of-distribution compared to the training data, indicating the model learns abstract patterns for classification.
Activation maximization with regularization terms is highly parameter-sensitive but can produce convincing results comparable to frequency-domain approaches.
Sequence Dreaming can reveal different learned representations by the model, including non-periodic patterns, which are not captured by frequency-domain methods.
papers.limitation:
Activation maximization with regularization terms is highly parameter-sensitive.
The generated time series are often out-of-distribution compared to the original training data.
future_direction: Exploring advanced regularization techniques, such as perturbations directed by attributions.
Adopting genetic or evolutionary algorithms for optimizing activation maximization.
Incorporating wavelet transforms for a richer representation of time series features.
papers.abstract: Understanding how models process and interpret time series data remains a significant challenge in deep learning to enable applicability in safety-critical areas such as healthcare. In this paper, we introduce Sequence Dreaming, a technique that adapts Activation Maximization to analyze sequential information, aiming to enhance the interpretability of neural networks operating on univariate time series. By leveraging this method, we visualize the temporal dynamics and patterns most influential in model decision-making processes. To counteract the generation of unrealistic or excessively noisy sequences, we enhance Sequence Dreaming with a range of regularization techniques, including exponential smoothing. This approach ensures the production of sequences that more accurately reflect the critical features identified by the neural network. Our approach is tested on a time series classification dataset encompassing applications in predictive maintenance. The results show that our proposed Sequence Dreaming approach demonstrates targeted activation maximization for different use cases so that either centered class or border activation maximization can be generated. The results underscore the versatility of Sequence Dreaming in uncovering salient temporal features learned by neural networks, thereby advancing model transparency and trustworthiness in decision-critical domains.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Transformers for Dynamical Systems
papers.research_question: What are the representational capabilities and limitations of single-layer Transformers for linear and nonlinear dynamical systems, and how do they relate to classical dynamical systems theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that softmax attention's convexity constraint limits representation of oscillatory linear dynamics, while for nonlinear systems with partial observability, attention acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism enabling state reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The success of attention-based models in dynamical systems forecasting depends critically on the interplay between the system’s spectral properties, the observation regime, and the model’s architectural constraints.
papers.key_findings:
For linear systems, the convexity constraint of softmax attention restricts the class of dynamics that can be represented, leading to oversmoothing in oscillatory settings.
For nonlinear systems under partial observability, attention acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism, enabling effective state reconstruction when sufficient temporal context and latent dimensionality are available.
Transformers can implicitly perform delay-coordinate embeddings, and the benefit of attention is most pronounced in partial observation regimes.
Positional encodings do not consistently benefit time-continuous physical systems and can lead to uniform averaging without them.
The latent dimension must exceed the intrinsic manifold dimension to allow proper unfolding of the attractor.
papers.limitation:
Softmax normalization enforces non-negativity and convexity that restrict representable dynamics.
Positional encodings do not consistently benefit time-continuous physical systems.
Latent dimension must exceed the intrinsic manifold dimension to allow proper unfolding before projection.
Analysis is limited to single-layer Transformers, and deeper architectures may exhibit different behaviors.
future_direction: Multi-head attention and multi-layer architectures to understand how multiple heads might specialize in distinct modes.
Mechanistic interpretability for stiff and multiscale systems to see if attention offers advantages in adaptive integration.
Shared latent space geometry in foundation models to understand how distinct dynamical behaviors are embedded.
papers.abstract: Transformers are increasingly adopted for modeling and forecasting time-series, yet their internal mechanisms remain poorly understood from a dynamical systems perspective. In contrast to classical autoregressive and state-space models, which benefit from well-established theoretical foundations, Transformer architectures are typically treated as black boxes. This gap becomes particularly relevant as attention-based models are considered for general-purpose or zero-shot forecasting across diverse dynamical regimes. In this work, we do not propose a new forecasting model, but instead investigate the representational capabilities and limitations of single-layer Transformers when applied to dynamical data. Building on a dynamical systems perspective we interpret causal self-attention as a linear, history-dependent recurrence and analyze how it processes temporal information. Through a series of linear and nonlinear case studies, we identify distinct operational regimes. For linear systems, we show that the convexity constraint imposed by softmax attention fundamentally restricts the class of dynamics that can be represented, leading to oversmoothing in oscillatory settings. For nonlinear systems under partial observability, attention instead acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism, enabling effective state reconstruction when sufficient temporal context and latent dimensionality are available. These results help bridge empirical observations with classical dynamical systems theory, providing insight into when and why Transformers succeed or fail as models of dynamical systems.

papers.title: Universal Redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms enable TSFMs to construct effective zero-shot forecasts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds universal redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), shows that middle layers are highly redundant and models are robust to ablations, and introduces an intrinsic head-pruning strategy based on stable rank to identify heads responsible for context parroting and seasonality bias.
papers.conclusion: The study sheds light on universal properties of TSFMs, revealing redundancies and providing an intrinsic head-pruning strategy that identifies heads responsible for common failure modes.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers in TSFMs are highly redundant and can be ablated with minimal performance drop.
An intrinsic head pruning strategy based on the stable rank of query-key projection matrices effectively identifies important heads.
Specific attention heads are responsible for degenerate phenomena such as context parroting and seasonality bias.
TSFMs exhibit significant variation in sensitivity to MLP ablations across architectures, with encoder-decoder models being more resilient.
The first and last layers are most important for model performance.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is technically limited to encoder-decoder models with causal masking.
The intrinsic head pruning strategy cannot account for the data-dependent exponential tilt term in the attention mechanism.
future_direction: Investigating how architecture determines what the transformer loads onto MLPs versus attention heads.
papers.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) leverage extensive pretraining to accurately predict unseen time series during inference, without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Through large-scale evaluations on standard benchmarks, we find that leading transformer-based TSFMs exhibit redundant components in their intermediate layers. We introduce a set of tools for mechanistic interpretability of TSFMs, including ablations of specific components and direct logit attribution on the residual stream. Our findings are consistent across several leading TSFMs with diverse architectures, and across a diverse set of real-world and synthetic time-series datasets. We discover that all models in our study are robust to ablations of entire layers. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical framework framing transformers as kernel regressors, motivating a purely intrinsic strategy for ablating heads based on the stable rank of the per-head projection matrices. Using this approach, we uncover the specific heads responsible for degenerate phenomena widely observed in TSFMs, such as parroting of motifs from the context and seasonality bias. Our study sheds light on the universal properties of this emerging class of architectures for continuous-time sequence modeling.

papers.title: Expressive architectures enhance interpretability of dynamics-based neural population models
papers.research_question: Does NODE-based sequential autoencoders more accurately and parsimoniously recover latent dynamical systems from simulated neural activity compared to RNN-based models?
papers.core_contribution: NODE-based sequential autoencoders can recover accurate and parsimonious latent dynamics from simulated neural activity, outperforming RNN-based models in interpretability.
papers.conclusion: NODE-based architectures are superior for interpretable neural population modeling due to their ability to learn accurate dynamics in low-dimensional latent spaces.
papers.key_findings:
NODE-based SAEs achieve similar reconstruction performance with fewer latent dimensions than GRU-based SAEs.
NODE-based SAEs have higher state R^2, indicating better recovery of true latent dynamics without superfluous features.
NODE-based SAEs more effectively recover fixed point properties and eigenvalues of the dynamical systems.
Ablation experiments show that skip connections and MLP capacity in NODEs are key to their superior performance.
RNN-based models struggle to recover accurate dynamics even when they have high reconstruction performance.
papers.limitation:
Global dynamics may be underdetermined from limited sampled trajectories, affecting fixed point recovery.
Models with best reconstruction performance may not concisely capture true dynamics, especially in chaotic systems.
Applicability to real neural data with time-varying dynamics and external inputs is uncertain.
future_direction: Extending the approach to real neural data with inputs and time-varying dynamics.
Testing recovery on partially observed and interacting dynamical systems.
Incorporating techniques from models like LFADS while preserving interpretability.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks that can recover latent dynamics from recorded neural activity may provide a powerful avenue for identifying and interpreting the dynamical motifs underlying biological computation. Given that neural variance alone does not uniquely determine a latent dynamical system, interpretable architectures should prioritize accurate and low-dimensional latent dynamics. In this work, we evaluated the performance of sequential autoencoders (SAEs) in recovering latent chaotic attractors from simulated neural datasets. We found that SAEs with widely-used recurrent neural network (RNN)-based dynamics were unable to infer accurate firing rates at the true latent state dimensionality, and that larger RNNs relied upon dynamical features not present in the data. On the other hand, SAEs with neural ordinary differential equation (NODE)-based dynamics inferred accurate rates at the true latent state dimensionality, while also recovering latent trajectories and fixed point structure. Ablations reveal that this is mainly because NODEs (1) allow use of higher-capacity multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to model the vector field and (2) predict the derivative rather than the next state. Decoupling the capacity of the dynamics model from its latent dimensionality enables NODEs to learn the requisite low-D dynamics where RNN cells fail. Additionally, the fact that the NODE predicts derivatives imposes a useful autoregressive prior on the latent states. The suboptimal interpretability of widely-used RNN-based dynamics may motivate substitution for alternative architectures, such as NODE, that enable learning of accurate dynamics in low-dimensional latent spaces.

papers.title: Explaining Time Series Predictions with Dynamic Masks
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of a machine learning model on multivariate time series data, addressing challenges like time dependency and large number of inputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Dynamask, a perturbation-based saliency method that produces instance-wise importance scores for each feature at each time step by fitting a dynamic mask to the input sequence, incorporating time dependency and parsimony for improved feature identification.
papers.conclusion: Dynamask addresses the challenges of explaining time series predictions by incorporating time dependency and parsimony, offering a neat improvement in feature importance identification and serving as a versatile tool for increasing model transparency.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamask improves the identification of feature importance over time compared to benchmark methods like Integrated Gradients, SHAP, and LIME.
The method's dynamic perturbation operators capture time context, leading to more accurate saliency maps.
Dynamask's parsimony and legibility, quantified via mask information and entropy, make it easier to interpret.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world clinical data show Dynamask's effectiveness in both regression and classification tasks.
The modularity of Dynamask allows it to be used as a plug-in for a wide range of machine learning models in areas like medicine and finance.
papers.abstract: How can we explain the predictions of a machine learning model? When the data is structured as a multivariate time series, this question induces additional difficulties such as the necessity for the explanation to embody the time dependency and the large number of inputs. To address these challenges, we propose dynamic masks (Dynamask). This method produces instance-wise importance scores for each feature at each time step by fitting a perturbation mask to the input sequence. In order to incorporate the time dependency of the data, Dynamask studies the effects of dynamic perturbation operators. In order to tackle the large number of inputs, we propose a scheme to make the feature selection parsimonious (to select no more feature than necessary) and legible (a notion that we detail by making a parallel with information theory). With synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate that the dynamic underpinning of Dynamask, together with its parsimony, offer a neat improvement in the identification of feature importance over time. The modularity of Dynamask makes it ideal as a plug-in to increase the transparency of a wide range of machine learning models in areas such as medicine and finance, where time series are abundant.

papers.title: FocusLearn: Fully-Interpretable, High-Performance Modular Neural Networks for Time Series
papers.research_question: How to build a fully-interpretable modular neural network for time series that matches or surpasses the predictive performance of non-interpretable deep networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FocusLearn, a fully-interpretable modular neural network for time series that uses attention for feature selection and node bootstrapping to achieve predictive performance comparable to non-interpretable deep networks.
papers.conclusion: FocusLearn achieves interpretability without sacrificing predictive performance, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art non-interpretable models on time series tasks.
papers.key_findings:
FocusLearn outperforms interpretable models (NAM and SPAM) on both regression and classification tasks across multiple metrics.
FocusLearn matches or surpasses the performance of non-interpretable models (LSTM and XGBoost) on the tested datasets.
The Attention-based Node Bootstrapping (ANB) and Attention-based Feature Selection (AFS) components are effective in improving predictive performance.
FocusLearn provides NAM-style interpretability with feature contribution plots.
Selecting a subset of features via AFS improves accuracy compared to using all features.
future_direction: Evaluate trade-offs such as the number of modules and feature interactions in practice.
Investigate the possibility of using attention to create higher-order feature interactions for implementation into a single network module.
Investigate the practical value of the explanations provided and how they may inform model intervention.
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series have had many applications in areas from healthcare and finance to meteorology and life sciences. Although deep neural networks have shown excellent predictive performance for time series, they have been criticised for being non-interpretable. Neural Additive Models, however, are known to be fully-interpretable by construction, but may achieve far lower predictive performance than deep networks when applied to time series. This paper introduces FocusLearn, a fully-interpretable modular neural network capable of matching or surpassing the predictive performance of deep networks trained on multivariate time series. In FocusLearn, a recurrent neural network learns the temporal dependencies in the data, while a multi-headed attention layer learns to weight selected features while also suppressing redundant features. Modular neural networks are then trained in parallel and independently, one for each selected feature. This modular approach allows the user to inspect how features influence outcomes in the exact same way as with additive models. Experimental results show that this new approach outperforms additive models in both regression and classification of time series tasks, achieving predictive performance that is comparable to state-of-the-art, non-interpretable deep networks applied to time series.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: FreqLens: Interpretable Frequency Attribution for Time Series Forecasting
papers.research_question: Can we design a forecasting model that (1) discovers dominant frequencies from data without prior knowledge, and (2) provides provably faithful attribution at the frequency level?
papers.core_contribution: We propose FreqLens, an interpretable forecasting framework that combines learnable frequency discovery with axiomatically grounded attribution, achieving competitive performance while discovering physically meaningful frequencies with formal theoretical guarantees.
papers.conclusion: FreqLens achieves genuine frequency-level knowledge discovery for time series forecasting with formal theoretical guarantees on attribution quality, demonstrating that interpretability does not have to come at the cost of performance.
papers.key_findings:
FreqLens achieves competitive or superior performance on Traffic and Weather datasets while discovering physically meaningful frequencies.
On Traffic, all 5 independent runs discover the 24-hour daily cycle (24.6 ± 0.1h, 2.5% error) and 12-hour half-daily cycle (11.8 ± 0.1h, 1.6% error) without domain knowledge.
On Weather, the model discovers weekly cycles (10× longer than the input window) from only 16 hours of input data.
The attribution framework satisfies four axioms (Completeness, Faithfulness, Null-Frequency, Symmetry) and is provably equivalent to Shapley values under the additive decomposition.
Ablation studies show the residual path and axiomatic attribution head are critical components, and the model is robust to hyperparameter choices like Gumbel temperature and number of frequency bases.
papers.limitation:
Performance degrades on non-periodic or strongly non-stationary time series where frequency decomposition is less effective.
Low-frequency discovery (weekly, monthly) is less consistent across seeds than high-frequency discovery (daily), suggesting the need for longer training or curriculum-based frequency learning.
The input sequence length constrains the maximum directly observable period; longer-period discovery relies on cross-batch gradient signals and is slower to converge.
future_direction: Cross-variable frequency interactions
Curriculum frequency learning
Non-stationary extensions combining learnable frequencies with trend decomposition
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting models often lack interpretability, limiting their adoption in domains requiring explainable predictions. We propose \textsc{FreqLens}, an interpretable forecasting framework that discovers and attributes predictions to learnable frequency components. \textsc{FreqLens} introduces two key innovations: (1) \emph{learnable frequency discovery} -- frequency bases are parameterized via sigmoid mapping and learned from data with diversity regularization, enabling automatic discovery of dominant periodic patterns without domain knowledge; and (2) \emph{axiomatic frequency attribution} -- a theoretically grounded framework that provably satisfies Completeness, Faithfulness, Null-Frequency, and Symmetry axioms, with per-frequency attributions equivalent to Shapley values. On Traffic and Weather datasets, \textsc{FreqLens} achieves competitive or superior performance while discovering physically meaningful frequencies: all 5 independent runs discover the 24-hour daily cycle ($24.6 \pm 0.1$h, 2.5\% error) and 12-hour half-daily cycle ($11.8 \pm 0.1$h, 1.6\% error) on Traffic, and weekly cycles ($10\times$ longer than the input window) on Weather. These results demonstrate genuine frequency-level knowledge discovery with formal theoretical guarantees on attribution quality.

papers.title: TimeSAE: Sparse Decoding for Faithful Explanations of Black-Box Time Series Models
papers.research_question: How can we provide faithful explanations for black-box time series models, especially under distribution shifts, by leveraging Sparse Autoencoders and causality?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TimeSAE, a framework for faithful explanations of black-box time series models using a Sparse Autoencoder to learn interpretable concepts and generate counterfactual explanations, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.
papers.conclusion: TimeSAE provides a faithful and interpretable explanation framework for black-box time series models, effectively handling distribution shifts and offering robust performance across diverse datasets and models.
papers.key_findings:
TimeSAE outperforms existing explanation baselines across multiple time series datasets and black-box models.
The method provides more faithful and robust explanations, particularly for out-of-distribution samples.
The use of JumpReLU and TopK activation functions in the SAE prevents dead concepts and improves learning stability.
The framework ensures compositional consistency and causal faithfulness through contrastive learning and regularization losses.
TimeSAE's explanations are model-agnostic and post-hoc, requiring no access to the internal structure of the black-box model.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on the dataset used to train the black-box models; performance may degrade with limited data.
Sensitivity to hyperparameter settings, such as sparsity levels and dictionary size.
papers.abstract: As black box models and pretrained models gain traction in time series applications, understanding and explaining their predictions becomes increasingly vital, especially in high-stakes domains where interpretability and trust are essential.
