However, most of the existing methods involve only in-distribution explanation, and do not generalize outside the training support, which requires the learning capability of generalization. In this work, we aim to provide a framework to explain black-box models for time series data through the dual lenses of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and causality. We show that many current explanation methods are sensitive to distributional shifts, limiting their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Building on the concept of Sparse Autoencoder, we introduce TimeSAE, a framework for black-box model explanation. We conduct extensive evaluations of TimeSAE on both synthetic and real-world time series datasets, comparing it to leading baselines. The results, supported by both quantitative metrics and qualitative insights, show that TimeSAE provides more faithful and robust explanations. Our code is available in an easy-to-use library TimeSAE-Lib: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/TimeSAE-571D/.

papers.title: Understanding Transformers for Time Series: Rank Structure, Flow-of-ranks, and Compressibility
papers.research_question: How well do community insights on pretraining and hyperparameter tuning, based largely on Transformers applied to text data, port to Transformers applied to other data modalities, specifically time series?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework for analyzing Transformers in time series through rank structure, showing that time-series embeddings are low-rank, which leads to compressible attention matrices, and introduces the flow-of-ranks concept to explain rank growth across layers, enabling effective compression of time series foundation models.
papers.conclusion: The rank structure framework provides principled guidance for allocating width, depth, and heads in time series foundation models and for exploiting their inherent compressibility, demonstrating significant practical compression gains.
papers.key_findings:
Time-series embeddings exhibit sharply decaying singular value spectra, making them low-rank compared to text or vision embeddings.
Attention layers on low-rank inputs admit accurate low-rank approximations, making them compressible.
Flow-of-ranks describes how nonlinear mixing across depth inflates rank, explaining why early layers are more compressible and ranks grow with depth.
Time series foundation models are highly compressible compared to language models of the same size.
Compressing Chronos reduces inference time by 65.4% and memory usage by 81.4% without loss of accuracy.
future_direction: Sparse parameterization of sketching matrices in head-dependent low-rank representations.
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely used across data modalities, and yet the principles distilled from text models often transfer imperfectly to models trained to other modalities. In this paper, we analyze Transformers through the lens of rank structure. Our focus is on the time series setting, where the structural properties of the data differ remarkably from those of text or vision. We show that time-series embeddings, unlike text or vision, exhibit sharply decaying singular value spectra: small patch sizes and smooth continuous mappings concentrate the data into low-rank subspaces. From this, we prove that the associated $Q/K/V$ projections admit accurate low-rank approximations, and that attention layers become compressible in proportion to the decay of the embedding spectrum. We introduce the concept of flow-of-ranks, a phenomenon by which nonlinear mixing across depth inflates the rank, explaining why early layers are most amenable to compression and why ranks grow with depth. Guided by these theoretical and empirical results, we use these insights to compress Chronos, a large time series foundation model, achieving a reduction of $65\%$ in inference time and $81\%$ in memory, without loss of accuracy. Our findings provide principled guidance for allocating width, depth, and heads in time series foundation models, and for exploiting their inherent compressibility.

papers.title: Why Attention Fails: The Degeneration of Transformers into MLPs in Time Series Forecasting
papers.research_question: Why do transformers underperform in time series forecasting, and why does the attention mechanism degenerate into MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that in time series transformers, attention mechanisms degenerate into MLPs because linear embeddings fail to provide a well-structured latent space, rendering attention ineffective.
papers.conclusion: The failure of attention in time series transformers is due to inadequate representation learning from linear embeddings, and future improvements should focus on learning better latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer blocks in time series models often degenerate into MLPs, with attention contributing minimally to performance.
Replacing attention matrices with zero, identity, or average matrices does not significantly affect model performance.
Perturbing the attention module has little impact, while perturbing the FFN module degrades performance, indicating that FFN is more critical.
Positional encoding is not effectively utilized in time series transformers, unlike in Vision Transformers (ViT).
Linear embedding layers are ineffective and unnecessary for time series data, as they fail to enable proper representation learning.
papers.limitation:
The degradation phenomenon may extend to other domains like classification and imputation, requiring further investigation.
Interpreting attention weights in time series data is complex due to lack of human comprehensibility, necessitating new metrics.
future_direction: Focus on improving representation learning before refining attention mechanisms.
Develop novel embeddings, such as using VQ-VAE or encoder-decoder architectures, for better latent spaces.
Create a new metric or benchmark to assess the influence of attention in time series models.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based architectures achieved high performance in natural language processing and computer vision, yet many studies have shown that they have not demonstrated a clear advantage in time series forecasting and even underperform simple linear baselines in some cases. However, most of these studies have not thoroughly explored the reasons behind the failure of transformers. To better understand time-series transformers(TST), we designed a series of experiments, progressively modifying transformers into MLPs to investigate the impact of the attention mechanism. Surprisingly, transformer blocks often degenerate into simple MLPs in existing time-series transformers. We designed a interpretable dataset to investigate the reasons behind the failure of the attention mechanism and revealed that the attention mechanism is not working in the expected way. We theoretically analyzed the reasons behind this phenomenon, demonstrating that the current embedding methods fail to allow transformers to function in a well-structured latent space, and further analyzed the deeper underlying causes of the failure of embedding.

papers.title: Dynamics of reservoir computing for crises prediction
papers.research_question: How does reservoir computing predict crises (discontinuous transitions) in dynamical systems? Specifically, what is the mechanism behind its successful prediction of boundary and attractor-merging crises?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a trained reservoir computing map can capture crises phenomena (boundary and attractor-merging crises) and reproduce the correct scaling behavior of transient lifetimes near the crisis point by mimicking the collision of chaotic attractors with unstable fixed points, as in the original dynamical system.
papers.conclusion: Reservoir computing can capture subtle transitions in chaotic dynamics, replicating crises phenomena and recovering the correct scaling behavior, but analyzing the mechanism in higher-dimensional systems presents significant challenges.
papers.key_findings:
The trained reservoir map reproduces attractor collisions with unstable fixed points, mimicking the actual system's crisis mechanism.
The reservoir learns the quadratic nonlinearity and invariant density responsible for the observed scaling behavior near the crisis point.
The trained reservoir correctly predicts the scaling exponent of the original system (e.g., logistic map, Gauss map).
The mechanism of crisis prediction via collision with unstable fixed points holds across distinct one-dimensional systems (logistic and Gauss maps).
In higher-dimensional systems (e.g., Hénon map), the crisis mechanism is more intricate and visualization of manifolds becomes challenging, though the reservoir still reproduces the crisis.
papers.limitation: Challenges in analyzing higher-dimensional systems due to difficulty in visualizing stable and unstable manifolds and identifying periodic orbits.
future_direction: Developing strategies to overcome the challenges of analyzing higher-dimensional systems to gain deeper insight into how data-driven models capture the mechanisms of discontinuous transitions.
papers.abstract: Reservoir computing has emerged as a powerful framework for time series modelling and forecasting including the prediction of discontinuous transitions. However, the mechanism behind its success is not yet fully understood. This letter elucidates the functioning of reservoir computing by examining its successful prediction of boundary and attractor merging crises. We investigate in detail how reservoirs's internal dynamics mimic the actual system, that enables it to accurately reproduce the scaling exponent near boundary crisis. We establish this across distinct systems, exemplified by the logistic and Gauss maps. The study contributes to the broader understanding of the internal dynamics that enable learning algorithms to anticipate critical transitions.

papers.title: An unexpected unity among methods for interpreting model predictions
papers.research_question: How can we interpret model predictions by estimating the importance of input features, and how does a model-agnostic additive representation based on Shapley values unify current methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a model-agnostic additive representation of feature importance based on Shapley values (ES values) unifies several existing interpretability methods (LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, Shapley regression values) and is the only solution satisfying key axioms of efficiency, symmetry, and monotonicity.
papers.conclusion: ES values provide a unified, axiomatically justified framework for interpreting model predictions, which can be used to improve existing methods and create novel visual explanations.
papers.key_findings:
ES values unify LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, and Shapley regression values under a single framework.
ES values are the only additive feature attribution method that satisfies the axioms of efficiency, symmetry, and monotonicity, providing an optimal solution.
The Shapley kernel derived from these axioms leads to more accurate and efficient estimation of feature importance compared to heuristically chosen kernels.
ES values provide theoretical justification for specific parameter choices in existing methods, such as the kernel for LIME and linearization for DeepLIFT.
ES values can be visualized to explain individual predictions and reveal patterns of model behavior across a dataset.
papers.abstract: Understanding why a model made a certain prediction is crucial in many data science fields. Interpretable predictions engender appropriate trust and provide insight into how the model may be improved. However, with large modern datasets the best accuracy is often achieved by complex models even experts struggle to interpret, which creates a tension between accuracy and interpretability. Recently, several methods have been proposed for interpreting predictions from complex models by estimating the importance of input features. Here, we present how a model-agnostic additive representation of the importance of input features unifies current methods. This representation is optimal, in the sense that it is the only set of additive values that satisfies important properties. We show how we can leverage these properties to create novel visual explanations of model predictions. The thread of unity that this representation weaves through the literature indicates that there are common principles to be learned about the interpretation of model predictions that apply in many scenarios.

papers.title: The geometry of BERT
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention mechanism work internally, and what insights can be gained about its classification process?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel theoretical perspective on BERT's attention mechanism, introducing the concepts of directionality of subspace selection and cone index, and analyzes attention patterns and global information flow to understand its classification process.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
The attention mechanism in BERT performs a subspace selection driven by the searching engine process (Q, K, V matrices).
The self-attention matrix exhibits specific, classifiable patterns (e.g., directional gate, open gate, contextual gates) that convey different types of information.
The cone index and distribution analysis show that lower layers specialize in finding information content, while upper layers primarily propagate it.
The information content propagates globally as a mean information content; the MLP synthesizes information from different heads, breaking the channel structure.
Rank collapse in attention is reinterpreted as a potential carrier of directional information rather than a purely negative phenomenon.
future_direction: Analysis of the BERT learning process during training.
Examining the specialization of individual components in the BERT architecture.
Leveraging these findings to optimize the architecture of the Transformer encoder.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks, particularly Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), have shown remarkable performance across various tasks such as classification, text summarization, and question answering. However, their internal mechanisms remain mathematically obscure, highlighting the need for greater explainability and interpretability. In this direction, this paper investigates the internal mechanisms of BERT proposing a novel perspective on the attention mechanism of BERT from a theoretical perspective. The analysis encompasses both local and global network behavior. At the local level, the concept of directionality of subspace selection as well as a comprehensive study of the patterns emerging from the self-attention matrix are presented. Additionally, this work explores the semantic content of the information stream through data distribution analysis and global statistical measures including the novel concept of cone index. A case study on the classification of SARS-CoV-2 variants using RNA which resulted in a very high accuracy has been selected in order to observe these concepts in an application. The insights gained from this analysis contribute to a deeper understanding of BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models and further analysis in the training process.

papers.title: Transformer Is Inherently a Causal Learner
papers.research_question: Can autoregressive transformers, trained for forecasting, inherently learn and reveal the causal structure of time series data through gradient sensitivities?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained autoregressively for next-step prediction naturally encode time-delayed causal structures, and gradient sensitivities (via Layer-wise Relevance Propagation) can recover the underlying causal graph without explicit causal objectives.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are inherently causal learners, and this connection opens a two-way bridge between causal discovery and foundation models, where causal principles can guide model improvement and foundation models enable scalable causal discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained for next-step prediction can recover the underlying causal graph from time series data via gradient attributions.
The method outperforms traditional causal discovery algorithms in high-dimensional, nonlinear, long-range dependency, and non-stationary settings.
Performance improves with increased data volume and heterogeneity, showing scaling potential where traditional methods lack.
Gradient-based attributions (LRP) are more reliable than raw attention weights for causal discovery.
The approach is robust to different noise distributions but degrades with latent variables.
papers.limitation: Lack of a mechanism for modeling latent variables and instantaneous effects.
future_direction: Handling latent confounders and instantaneous relationships.
Integrating known domain indicators to improve data efficiency in non-stationary settings.
Applying the method to real-world data and exploring the use of causal principles to improve foundation models.
papers.abstract: We reveal that transformers trained in an autoregressive manner naturally encode time-delayed causal structures in their learned representations. When predicting future values in multivariate time series, the gradient sensitivities of transformer outputs with respect to past inputs directly recover the underlying causal graph, without any explicit causal objectives or structural constraints. We prove this connection theoretically under standard identifiability conditions and develop a practical extraction method using aggregated gradient attributions. On challenging cases such as nonlinear dynamics, long-term dependencies, and non-stationary systems, this approach greatly surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art discovery algorithms, especially as data heterogeneity increases, exhibiting scaling potential where causal accuracy improves with data volume and heterogeneity, a property traditional methods lack. This unifying view lays the groundwork for a future paradigm where causal discovery operates through the lens of foundation models, and foundation models gain interpretability and enhancement through the lens of causality.

papers.title: Analyzing Deep Transformer Models for Time Series Forecasting via Manifold Learning
papers.research_question: How do geometric features (intrinsic dimension and curvature) of latent representations in transformer-based time series forecasting models change across layers, correlate with performance, and evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer-based time series forecasting models exhibit consistent geometric profiles in their latent manifolds, with intrinsic dimension and curvature patterns that correlate with model performance, providing a new perspective for model analysis and design.
papers.conclusion: Manifold learning provides a valuable framework for analyzing transformer-based time series forecasting models, revealing geometric patterns and correlations that can guide the development of improved forecasting architectures.
papers.key_findings:
During encoding, intrinsic dimension and curvature decrease or remain fixed, while during decoding they increase.
Geometric profiles are similar across different architectures, datasets, and forecast horizons.
Mean absolute principal curvature (MAPC) in the final layer is positively correlated with test mean squared error, indicating lower error with lower curvature.
Untrained models exhibit random geometric profiles that converge rapidly within a few epochs of training.
Datasets with underlying correlations (e.g., weather and electricity transformer temperature) show similar geometric features.
future_direction: Deeper investigation of classification versus regression from a manifold learning perspective.
Design of deeper and more expressive time series forecasting models.
papers.abstract: Transformer models have consistently achieved remarkable results in various domains such as natural language processing and computer vision. However, despite ongoing research efforts to better understand these models, the field still lacks a comprehensive understanding. This is particularly true for deep time series forecasting methods, where analysis and understanding work is relatively limited. Time series data, unlike image and text information, can be more challenging to interpret and analyze. To address this, we approach the problem from a manifold learning perspective, assuming that the latent representations of time series forecasting models lie next to a low-dimensional manifold. In our study, we focus on analyzing the geometric features of these latent data manifolds, including intrinsic dimension and principal curvatures. Our findings reveal that deep transformer models exhibit similar geometric behavior across layers, and these geometric features are correlated with model performance. Additionally, we observe that untrained models initially have different structures, but they rapidly converge during training. By leveraging our geometric analysis and differentiable tools, we can potentially design new and improved deep forecasting neural networks. This approach complements existing analysis studies and contributes to a better understanding of transformer models in the context of time series forecasting. Code is released at https://github.com/azencot-group/GATLM.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Concept Extraction for Time Series with ECLAD-ts
papers.research_question: How can we provide post-hoc global explanations for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in time series classification by automatically extracting and localizing concepts from the model's internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces ECLAD-ts, a novel concept extraction and localization method specifically designed for time series data. It extracts concepts by clustering timestep-wise aggregations of CNN activation maps (Local Aggregated Descriptors) and computes channel-wise importance scores using model gradients, providing post-hoc global explanations that capture temporal and channel-specific information.
papers.conclusion: ECLAD-ts represents a step toward better understanding the decision-making processes of CNNs for time series classification, enhancing model transparency and trust. It effectively extracts and localizes concepts, providing valuable insights into model behavior and alignment with human expectations.
papers.key_findings:
ECLAD-ts effectively extracts meaningful concepts that align with ground truth primitives in synthetic datasets, localizing them both temporally and across channels.
The method's importance scoring mechanism correctly identifies concepts used for classification and can reveal shortcut learning, where models rely on background features instead of intended primitives.
ECLAD-ts outperforms benchmark methods (ECLAD, ConceptShap, MultiVISION) in terms of representation correctness and importance correctness on both synthetic and natural datasets.
The extracted concepts provide insights into the model's general prediction process and can explain individual classifications, including misclassifications.
Concepts are distinctively encoded in the latent space of CNNs, and ECLAD-ts leverages this to produce human-understandable explanations.
papers.limitation:
Visualization of complex features in the time series domain can be problematic.
All considered concept extraction methods exhibit sensitivity to hyperparameter settings, especially the number of concepts.
Concept compositionality and correlation, a common phenomenon in time series, is not fully addressed.
future_direction: Refining visualization techniques and developing more adaptive methods to handle hyperparameter sensitivity.
Exploring concept compositionality and correlation in the context of concept extraction for time series.
Investigating the integration of concept extraction into real-time model training and modifying other methods (e.g., ConceptShap, MultiVISION) to work properly in the time series domain.
papers.abstract: Abstract Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for time series classification (TSC) are being increasingly used in applications ranging from quality prediction to medical diagnosis. The black box nature of these models makes understanding their prediction process difficult. This issue is crucial because CNNs are prone to learning shortcuts and biases, compromising their robustness and alignment with human expectations. To assess whether such mechanisms are being used and the associated risk, it is essential to provide model explanations that reflect the inner workings of the model. Concept Extraction (CE) methods offer such explanations, but have mostly been developed for the image domain so far, leaving a gap in the time series domain. In this work, we present a CE and localization method tailored to the time series domain, based on the ideas of CE methods for images. We propose the novel method ECLAD-ts, which provides post-hoc global explanations based on how the models encode subsets of the input at different levels of abstraction. For this, concepts are produced by clustering timestep-wise aggregations of CNN activation maps, and their importance is computed based on their impact on the prediction process. We evaluate our method on synthetic and natural datasets. Furthermore, we assess the advantages and limitations of CE in time series through empirical results. Our results show that ECLAD-ts effectively explains models by leveraging their internal representations, providing useful insights about their prediction process.

papers.title: On the Mechanistic Interpretability of Neural Networks for Causality in Bio-statistics
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability techniques be transposed to bio-statistics, and how effective are they?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability tools can be leveraged to probe and validate internal representations learned by neural networks for causal inference, discover and visualize computational pathways for confounders and treatments, and compare learned mechanisms across model types.
papers.abstract: Interpretable insights from predictive models remain critical in bio-statistics, particularly when assessing causality, where classical statistical and machine learning methods often provide inherent clarity. While Neural Networks (NNs) offer powerful capabilities for modeling complex biological data, their traditional "black-box" nature presents challenges for validation and trust in high-stakes health applications. Recent advances in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aim to decipher the internal computations learned by these networks. This work investigates the application of MI techniques to NNs within the context of causal inference for bio-statistics. We demonstrate that MI tools can be leveraged to: (1) probe and validate the internal representations learned by NNs, such as those estimating nuisance functions in frameworks like Targeted Minimum Loss-based Estimation (TMLE); (2) discover and visualize the distinct computational pathways employed by the network to process different types of inputs, potentially revealing how confounders and treatments are handled; and (3) provide methodologies for comparing the learned mechanisms and extracted insights across statistical, machine learning, and NN models, fostering a deeper understanding of their respective strengths and weaknesses for causal bio-statistical analysis.

papers.title: Delta-XAI: A Unified Framework for Explaining Prediction Changes in Online Time Series Monitoring
papers.research_question: How can we explain prediction changes (differences between adjacent time steps) in online time series monitoring models, rather than explaining single predictions in isolation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Delta-XAI, a unified framework for explaining prediction changes in online time series monitoring, which includes a wrapper to adapt existing single-prediction XAI methods and introduces SWING, a novel gradient-based method that extends Integrated Gradients to capture temporal dependencies.
papers.conclusion: SWING provides effective, efficient, and clinically coherent explanations for prediction changes in online time series monitoring, outperforming existing methods across a range of benchmarks and metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Classical gradient-based methods like Integrated Gradients (IG) perform well when adapted via the Delta-XAI wrapper for explaining prediction changes.
The proposed SWING method, which incorporates past observations via shifted window integration paths, outperforms existing XAI methods across diverse datasets and model architectures.
The paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation suite for online time series XAI, assessing faithfulness, sufficiency, coherence, and efficiency.
papers.limitation:
SWING introduces additional computational overhead compared to simpler methods like standard Integrated Gradients.
The prediction wrapper function may require minor adjustments for some existing XAI algorithms that rely on probability outputs or internal model representations.
papers.abstract: Explaining online time series monitoring models is crucial across sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance, where temporal and contextual prediction dynamics underpin critical decisions. While recent XAI methods have improved the explainability of time series models, they mostly analyze each time step independently, overlooking temporal dependencies. This results in further challenges: explaining prediction changes is non-trivial, methods fail to leverage online dynamics, and evaluation remains difficult. To address these challenges, we propose Delta-XAI, which adapts 14 existing XAI methods through a wrapper function and introduces a principled evaluation suite for the online setting, assessing diverse aspects, such as faithfulness, sufficiency, and coherence. Experiments reveal that classical gradient-based methods, such as Integrated Gradients (IG), can outperform recent approaches when adapted for temporal analysis. Building on this, we propose Shifted Window Integrated Gradients (SWING), which incorporates past observations in the integration path to systematically capture temporal dependencies and mitigate out-of-distribution effects. Extensive experiments consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of SWING across diverse settings with respect to diverse metrics. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Delta-XAI.

papers.title: Beyond Sparsity: Tree Regularization of Deep Models for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can we create deep models that are well-approximated by compact, human-simulatable models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces tree regularization, a method to train deep models so their predictions are closely approximated by small decision trees, improving interpretability without sacrificing predictive accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Tree regularization is an effective method for training deep models to be more interpretable by ensuring their predictions can be approximated by compact decision trees, enabling human simulability.
papers.key_findings:
Tree regularization yields models with decision boundaries that are simpler (shorter average path length in approximating decision trees) than those regularized with L1 or L2 penalties.
Tree-regularized models achieve a better trade-off between prediction accuracy (AUC) and complexity (average path length) than L1 or L2 regularized models.
The method is effective on both synthetic tasks (2D Parabola, Signal-and-noise HMM) and real-world medical and speech tasks (Sepsis, HIV, TIMIT).
The approximate decision trees for tree-regularized models are useful for human simulation and interpretability.
Standalone decision trees are less accurate than tree-regularized deep models.
papers.abstract: The lack of interpretability remains a key barrier to the adoption of deep models in many applications. In this work, we explicitly regularize deep models so human users might step through the process behind their predictions in little time. Specifically, we train deep time-series models so their class-probability predictions have high accuracy while being closely modeled by decision trees with few nodes. Using intuitive toy examples as well as medical tasks for treating sepsis and HIV, we demonstrate that this new tree regularization yields models that are easier for humans to simulate than simpler L1 or L2 penalties without sacrificing predictive power.

papers.title: Extracting Interpretable Local and Global Representations from Attention on Time Series
papers.research_question: How can interpretable local and global representations be extracted from transformer attention mechanisms for time series data?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents two transformer attention-based interpretability methods (LASA and GCR) for time series data, providing a framework for local abstraction and global representation that improves interpretability/complexity while maintaining performance similar to the baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the presented methods are effective for extracting interpretable local and global representations from attention on time series data, and provides guidance for their application.
papers.key_findings:
The presented LASA and GCR approaches demonstrate a significant improvement in interpretability/complexity while capturing many core decisions and maintaining similar performance to the baseline model.
The methods provide a comprehensive framework for both local and global interpretation of attention on time series data.
Experiments on univariate datasets from the UCR UEA repository show the efficacy of the approaches, with extensive hyperparameter analysis.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is currently only adapted to univariate data; multivariate data opens up further challenges, e.g., differentiating attention between sequences and/or considering cross-sequential influence.
future_direction: Extending the methods to handle multivariate time series data.
papers.abstract: This paper targets two transformer attention based interpretability methods working with local abstraction and global representation, in the context of time series data. We distinguish local and global contexts, and provide a comprehensive framework for both general interpretation options. We discuss their specific instantiation via different methods in detail, also outlining their respective computational implementation and abstraction variants. Furthermore, we provide extensive experimentation demonstrating the efficacy of the presented approaches. In particular, we perform our experiments using a selection of univariate datasets from the UCR UEA time series repository where we both assess the performance of the proposed approaches, as well as their impact on explainability and interpretability/complexity. Here, with an extensive analysis of hyperparameters, the presented approaches demonstrate an significant improvement in interpretability/complexity, while capturing many core decisions of and maintaining a similar performance to the baseline model. Finally, we draw general conclusions outlining and guiding the application of the presented methods.

papers.title: TimeSliver : Symbolic-Linear Decomposition for Explainable Time Series Classification
papers.research_question: How can we assign meaningful positive and negative importance scores to each temporal segment in time series classification to explain model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TimeSliver, a deep learning framework that linearly combines raw time series with symbolic abstraction to construct a representation that enables computation of positive and negative temporal attribution scores for each time point.
papers.conclusion: TimeSliver is an effective framework for explainable time series classification, providing high predictive performance and interpretable temporal attribution scores.
papers.key_findings:
TimeSliver outperforms other temporal attribution methods by 11% on 7 synthetic and real-world datasets.
TimeSliver achieves predictive performance within 2% of state-of-the-art baselines across 26 UEA benchmark datasets.
TimeSliver provides both positive and negative attribution scores, offering a complete explanation of model predictions.
The use of symbolic representation (Z) is crucial for scale-invariant attribution, with raw input projection leading to a 38% drop in explainability.
TimeSliver effectively captures far-field multiplicative interactions in temporal data.
future_direction: Human-in-the-loop expert validation for practical applications like sleep-stage classification.
Extending TimeSliver's principles to provide feature attribution, identifying influential input features at each time segment.
papers.abstract: Identifying the extent to which every temporal segment influences a model's predictions is essential for explaining model decisions and increasing transparency. While post-hoc explainable methods based on gradients and feature-based attributions have been popular, they suffer from reference state sensitivity and struggle to generalize across time-series datasets, as they treat time points independently and ignore sequential dependencies. Another perspective on explainable time-series classification is through interpretable components of the model, for instance, leveraging self-attention mechanisms to estimate temporal attribution; however, recent findings indicate that these attention weights often fail to provide faithful measures of temporal importance. In this work, we advance this perspective and present a novel explainability-driven deep learning framework, TimeSliver, which jointly utilizes raw time-series data and its symbolic abstraction to construct a representation that maintains the original temporal structure. Each element in this representation linearly encodes the contribution of each temporal segment to the final prediction, allowing us to assign a meaningful importance score to every time point. For time-series classification, TimeSliver outperforms other temporal attribution methods by 11% on 7 distinct synthetic and real-world multivariate time-series datasets. TimeSliver also achieves predictive performance within 2% of state-of-the-art baselines across 26 UEA benchmark datasets, positioning it as a strong and explainable framework for general time-series classification.

papers.title: Deconstructing Recurrence, Attention, and Gating: Investigating the transferability of Transformers and Gated Recurrent Neural Networks in forecasting of dynamical systems
papers.research_question: What are the key architectural components (gating, attention, recurrence) that enable forecasting accuracy in Transformers and RNNs, and how can they be combined to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neural gating and attention improve RNNs, while recurrence harms Transformers, and that a hybrid architecture combining Recurrent Highway Networks with gating and attention performs best for spatiotemporal forecasting.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that core mechanisms like gating, attention, and recurrence should be treated as hyperparameters and tuned for each task, leading to improved forecasting performance, with the best architecture being a hybrid Recurrent Highway Network with gating and attention.
papers.key_findings:
Neural gating and attention improve the performance of standard RNNs in most forecasting tasks.
Adding recurrence to Transformers is detrimental to their forecasting performance.
A hybrid architecture integrating Recurrent Highway Networks with neural gating and attention mechanisms emerges as the best performing model for high-dimensional spatiotemporal forecasting.
Transformers train faster than RNNs but RNNs achieve higher forecasting accuracy.
The effectiveness of gating mechanisms (coupled vs. uncoupled) is task-dependent.
papers.abstract: Machine learning architectures, including transformers and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have revolutionized forecasting in applications ranging from text processing to extreme weather. Notably, advanced network architectures, tuned for applications such as natural language processing, are transferable to other tasks such as spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. However, there is a scarcity of ablation studies to illustrate the key components that enable this forecasting accuracy. The absence of such studies, although explainable due to the associated computational cost, intensifies the belief that these models ought to be considered as black boxes. In this work, we decompose the key architectural components of the most powerful neural architectures, namely gating and recurrence in RNNs, and attention mechanisms in transformers. Then, we synthesize and build novel hybrid architectures from the standard blocks, performing ablation studies to identify which mechanisms are effective for each task. The importance of considering these components as hyper-parameters that can augment the standard architectures is exhibited on various forecasting datasets, from the spatiotemporal chaotic dynamics of the multiscale Lorenz 96 system, the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, as well as standard real world time-series benchmarks. A key finding is that neural gating and attention improves the performance of all standard RNNs in most tasks, while the addition of a notion of recurrence in transformers is detrimental. Furthermore, our study reveals that a novel, sparsely used, architecture which integrates Recurrent Highway Networks with neural gating and attention mechanisms, emerges as the best performing architecture in high-dimensional spatiotemporal forecasting of dynamical systems.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: TSInsight: A local-global attribution framework for interpretability in time-series data
papers.research_question: How can we provide interpretability for deep learning models on time-series data through a local-global attribution framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TSInsight, a novel attribution method for time-series data that attaches an auto-encoder to a classifier and fine-tunes it with a sparsity-inducing norm and reconstruction penalty to highlight features important for prediction, providing both instance-based and model-based explanations.
papers.conclusion: TSInsight is an effective method for interpretability of deep time-series models, providing intelligible and reliable feature attributions with properties like output space contraction and generic applicability.
papers.key_findings:
TSInsight produces sparse and aligned attributions that highlight salient regions of the input for time-series classification.
TSInsight can outperform the pretrained classifier in accuracy on most datasets when hyperparameters are carefully tuned.
TSInsight is competitive with other attribution methods in suppression tests and provides more plausible explanations.
TSInsight induces a contraction in the input space, as shown by Jacobian spectrum analysis.
TSInsight is applicable to different base architectures (CNN and LSTM) and provides both instance-based and model-based explanations.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter selection is primitive and needs further investigation for wide-scale applicability.
Gains in adversarial robustness are not consistent and require further study.
future_direction: Automated selection of hyperparameters.
Further investigation of the impact on adversarial robustness.
papers.abstract: With the rise in the employment of deep learning methods in safety-critical scenarios, interpretability is more essential than ever before. Although many different directions regarding interpretability have been explored for visual modalities, time-series data has been neglected with only a handful of methods tested due to their poor intelligibility. We approach the problem of interpretability in a novel way by proposing TSInsight where we attach an auto-encoder to the classifier with a sparsity-inducing norm on its output and fine-tune it based on the gradients from the classifier and a reconstruction penalty. TSInsight learns to preserve features that are important for prediction by the classifier and suppresses those that are irrelevant i.e. serves as a feature attribution method to boost interpretability. In contrast to most other attribution frameworks, TSInsight is capable of generating both instance-based and model-based explanations. We evaluated TSInsight along with 9 other commonly used attribution methods on 8 different time-series datasets to validate its efficacy. Evaluation results show that TSInsight naturally achieves output space contraction, therefore, is an effective tool for the interpretability of deep time-series models.

papers.title: Shaping Dynamics With Multiple Populations in Low-Rank Recurrent Networks
papers.research_question: How does the connectivity structure (rank and population structure) of a low-rank recurrent neural network determine the emergent dynamical system?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gaussian-mixture low-rank recurrent networks and shows that the rank sets the dimensionality of the dynamics while the population structure shapes the dynamics, and that with enough populations, such networks can approximate any dynamical system.
papers.conclusion: Gaussian-mixture low-rank networks provide a theoretical framework for understanding how connectivity structure determines emergent dynamics, with the rank setting dimensionality and population structure shaping the dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
In autonomous networks of rank R, the dynamics are characterized by R collective variables that form a dynamical system.
The dynamics can be described by an effective circuit of interacting collective variables with gain-modulated effective couplings.
A rank R network with a sufficient number of populations can approximate any R-dimensional dynamical system over a bounded domain.
Networks with a single Gaussian population have limited dynamics, supporting at most two stable fixed points regardless of rank.
Adding multiple populations allows for multiple stable fixed points and more complex dynamics, such as limit cycles and arbitrary fixed point arrangements.
papers.limitation:
The universal approximation theorem does not specify how many populations are needed to approximate a given dynamical system, nor does it provide an algorithm for finding the population statistics.
The approximation of arbitrary vector fields over the full domain requires the vector field to follow asymptotic leaky dynamics for large input values.
future_direction: Investigate how connectivity statistics could be adjusted through learning to implement specific computations.
Explore how population structure could emerge from plasticity rules.
papers.abstract: An emerging paradigm proposes that neural computations can be understood at the level of dynamic systems that govern low-dimensional trajectories of collective neural activity. How the connectivity structure of a network determines the emergent dynamical system, however, remains to be clarified. Here we consider a novel class of models, gaussian-mixture, low-rank recurrent networks in which the rank of the connectivity matrix and the number of statistically defined populations are independent hyperparameters. We show that the resulting collective dynamics form a dynamical system, where the rank sets the dimensionality and the population structure shapes the dynamics. In particular, the collective dynamics can be described in terms of a simplified effective circuit of interacting latent variables. While having a single global population strongly restricts the possible dynamics, we demonstrate that if the number of populations is large enough, a rank R network can approximate any R-dimensional dynamical system.

papers.title: Visualising Deep Network's Time-Series Representations
papers.research_question: How to visualize the internal time-series representations learned by deep learning classification models to provide insight into model behavior and aid in model selection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method for visualizing the internal time-series representations of deep learning models by combining a trained classifier with parametric t-SNE, showing it provides more discernible visualizations than PCA and unsupervised t-SNE, and that visualization quality can indicate classification performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method provides high-quality, intuitive visualizations of internal time-series representations from deep learning models, which can help understand model behavior and assist in model selection.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method combining a classifier with parametric t-SNE provides better visualizations than using PCA or unsupervised t-SNE alone.
Fine-tuning the combined model (classifier + t-SNE network) end-to-end significantly improves visualization quality compared to using a fixed classifier.
The quality of the visualization (measured by trustworthiness and 3-NN score) is related to the classification performance of the underlying model, with better classifiers generally producing better visualizations.
The TABL network performed best in classification and also produced the best visualizations among the tested models.
End-to-end unsupervised training of a parametric t-SNE network (without a pre-trained classifier) was ineffective for the financial time-series data, producing poor visualizations.
papers.limitation: Visualizing tens of thousands of time-series data points in a low-dimensional space can lead to cluttered and unreadable plots.
future_direction: Exploitation of time-series data representations over successive training epochs for guiding the training process.
Creation of multi-scale time-series data visualisations by connecting representations obtained from multiple layers of the classification model.
Creation of hybrid 3-dimensional data visualisations corresponding to the 2-dimensional visualisation of the model’s response over the instances of the input time-series.
papers.abstract: Despite the popularisation of machine learning models, more often than not, they still operate as black boxes with no insight into what is happening inside the model. There exist a few methods that allow to visualise and explain why a model has made a certain prediction. Those methods, however, allow visualisation of the link between the input and output of the model without presenting how the model learns to represent the data used to train the model as whole. In this paper, a method that addresses that issue is proposed, with a focus on visualising multi-dimensional time-series data. Experiments on a high-frequency stock market dataset show that the method provides fast and discernible visualisations. Large datasets can be visualised quickly and on one plot, which makes it easy for a user to compare the learned representations of the data. The developed method successfully combines known techniques to provide an insight into the inner workings of time-series classification models.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
papers.research_question: How can we unify existing methods for interpreting model predictions and assign feature importance values that satisfy desirable properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SHAP, a unified framework for interpreting model predictions that unifies six existing methods and provides a unique solution with desirable properties, leading to new methods with improved computational performance and consistency with human intuition.
papers.conclusion: The SHAP framework identifies the class of additive feature importance methods and shows there is a unique solution in this class that adheres to desirable properties, providing a unified approach to model interpretation with improved estimation methods.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP unifies six existing feature attribution methods: LIME, DeepLIFT, Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values, and Quantitative Input Influence.
SHAP values are the unique solution in the class of additive feature attribution methods that satisfy local accuracy, missingness, and consistency.
Kernel SHAP provides more accurate estimates with fewer model evaluations than previous sampling-based methods like Shapley sampling values.
SHAP values are more consistent with human intuition than LIME and DeepLIFT in user studies on simple models.
Deep SHAP, a compositional approximation for deep networks, improves upon DeepLIFT by better approximating Shapley values.
papers.limitation: Exact computation of SHAP values is challenging and requires approximations, which may rely on assumptions like feature independence or model linearity.
future_direction: Developing faster model-type-specific estimation methods that make fewer assumptions.
Integrating work on estimating interaction effects from game theory.
Defining new explanation model classes.
papers.abstract: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Concepts: Unifying Causal Representation Learning and Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can we learn human-interpretable concepts from data by unifying causal representation learning and foundation models, and under what conditions are such concepts identifiable?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unifies causal representation learning and foundation models by formally defining concepts as affine subspaces in latent representation spaces, proving near-optimal identifiability guarantees for concept learning with only n+2 environments, and applying this framework to explain and improve inference-time intervention for aligning LLMs towards truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a unified framework for learning interpretable concepts that bridges causal representation learning and foundation models, providing identifiability guarantees and demonstrating practical utility in improving LLM alignment via enhanced inference-time steering.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts defined as affine subspaces are identifiable up to linear transformations with only n+2 environments, a significant reduction compared to traditional CRL which requires dimension-dependent environments.
A contrastive learning algorithm validates the identifiability theory on synthetic data with concept conditional distributions.
The framework explains why inference-time intervention (ITI) steering vectors work for truthfulness in LLMs and proposes using steering matrices for better alignment, showing improved performance on TruthfulQA with LLaMA.
papers.abstract: To build intelligent machine learning systems, there are two broad approaches. One approach is to build inherently interpretable models, as endeavored by the growing field of causal representation learning. The other approach is to build highly-performant foundation models and then invest efforts into understanding how they work. In this work, we relate these two approaches and study how to learn human-interpretable concepts from data. Weaving together ideas from both fields, we formally define a notion of concepts and show that they can be provably recovered from diverse data. Experiments on synthetic data and large language models show the utility of our unified approach.

papers.title: Neural Earthquake Forecasting with Minimal Information: Limits, Interpretability, and the Role of Markov Structure
papers.research_question: Can neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting generalize temporally when trained on early data and tested on future unseen events?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hybrid neural-Markov model for earthquake forecasting and a temporal cross-validation framework, showing that model performance degrades on future data due to non-stationarity, highlighting the importance of temporal evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting fail to generalize to future data due to temporal non-stationarity, highlighting the need for temporally realistic evaluation and caution in applying machine learning to sparse forecasting settings.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model outperforms the Markov baseline on validation data but fails to generalize to the most recent quintile of the catalog.
The final quintile of seismicity exhibits more Markov-consistent behavior than earlier data, indicating temporal non-stationarity.
Integrated Gradients attribution shows a shift in feature importance between validation and test sets, with magnitude features becoming more relevant in the test set.
Temporal cross-validation reveals that model performance is highly dependent on the temporal location of the test data, with the last quintile consistently underperforming.
The study underscores the risk of overfitting to early patterns and the need for temporally realistic benchmarks in earthquake forecasting.
papers.limitation:
Small sample size affects all statistical models based on this data.
Sparse input features limited to simple descriptors of past events restrict the models' ability to capture complex physical dynamics.
The Markov prior is static and unable to account for possible changes in seismic regimes.
Results are based on a single regional earthquake catalog without additional geophysical or contextual data.
Only feedforward architectures were considered; models with more explicit temporal reasoning were not explored.
future_direction: Refine the use of prior knowledge with dynamic extensions of the Markov model or hierarchical priors that adapt across segments of the catalog.
Incorporate additional physical variables such as fault-specific information, geodetic signals, or stress evolution proxies.
Explore dynamically updated models or time-aware architectures to track evolving patterns more effectively.
papers.abstract: Abstract Forecasting earthquake sequences remains a central challenge in seismology, particularly under non-stationary conditions. While deep learning models have shown promise, their ability to generalize across time remains poorly understood. We evaluate neural and hybrid (NN + Markov) models for short-term earthquake forecasting on a regional catalog using temporally stratified cross-validation. Models are trained on earlier portions of the catalog and evaluated on future unseen events, enabling realistic assessment of temporal generalization. We find that while these models outperform a purely Markovian model on validation data, their test performance degrades substantially in the most recent quintile. A detailed attribution analysis reveals a shift in feature relevance over time, with later data exhibiting simpler, more Markov-consistent behavior. To support interpretability, we apply Integrated Gradients, a type of explainable AI (XAI) to analyze how models rely on different input features. These results highlight the risks of overfitting to early patterns in seismicity and underscore the importance of temporally realistic benchmarks. We conclude that forecasting skill is inherently time-dependent and benefits from combining physical priors with data-driven methods.

papers.title: Relative Geometry of Neural Forecasters: Linking Accuracy and Alignment in Learned Latent Geometry
papers.research_question: How do neural forecasters internally represent dynamical systems, and does the alignment of their latent geometries across model families correlate with forecasting accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces anchor-based relative embeddings to compare latent spaces of neural forecasters, revealing family-level alignment patterns and showing that alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
papers.conclusion: Relative geometry provides a reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize dynamical structure, and alignment offers insights beyond task loss.
papers.key_findings:
Anchor-based relative embeddings remove rotational and scaling ambiguities, enabling direct comparison of latent spaces across model families.
MLPs align with other MLPs, RNNs with RNNs, while transformers and ESNs achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment.
Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
The alignment signal stabilizes with increasing number of anchors (K>=16).
Noise and input length affect representational stability differently across forecasters.
papers.limitation: Alignment with the 'true system' refers only to alignment with the relative representation of observed trajectories, not to recovery of governing equations or physical state variables.
future_direction: Developing bridging mappings between model families
Alignment-driven training interventions
papers.abstract: Neural networks can accurately forecast complex dynamical systems, yet how they internally represent underlying latent geometry remains poorly understood. We study neural forecasters through the lens of representational alignment, introducing anchor-based, geometry-agnostic relative embeddings that remove rotational and scaling ambiguities in latent spaces. Applying this framework across seven canonical dynamical systems - ranging from periodic to chaotic - we reveal reproducible family-level structure: multilayer perceptrons align with other MLPs, recurrent networks with RNNs, while transformers and echo-state networks achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment. Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, yet high accuracy can coexist with low alignment. Relative geometry thus provides a simple, reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize and represent dynamical structure.

papers.title: Probing the Relationship Between Latent Linear Dynamical Systems and Low-Rank Recurrent Neural Network Models
papers.research_question: When can latent linear dynamical system (LDS) models be converted to low-rank linear recurrent neural network (RNN) models, and vice versa?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that latent LDS models are non-Markovian and cannot generally be converted to low-rank linear RNNs, but can be approximated by RNNs in specific limits (e.g., large number of neurons, orthogonal observation noise). Conversely, any linear low-rank RNN can be mapped to a latent LDS model with latent dimensionality at most twice the rank of the RNN.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes the mathematical relationship between latent LDS and low-rank linear RNN models, showing their equivalence in limit cases and providing mappings between them, which opens the door to comparing different fitting approaches and developing new inference methods.
papers.key_findings:
Latent LDS models generate non-Markovian observation sequences, while low-rank linear RNNs are strictly Markovian.
A latent LDS can be approximated by a low-rank linear RNN that matches its first-order marginals, with the approximation becoming exact when the observation noise is orthogonal to the latent subspace or in the limit of a large number of neurons relative to the latent dimensionality.
Any linear low-rank RNN can be converted to an equivalent latent LDS model, with the latent space dimension at most twice the rank of the RNN's connectivity matrix.
The two model classes are closely related, with linear low-rank RNNs comprising a subset of the broader class of latent LDS models.
The relationship provides a foundation for comparing different fitting approaches for these models and for developing probabilistic methods to infer RNN parameters from data.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to linear models.
future_direction: Developing probabilistic methods for inferring RNN parameters from data by leveraging the relationship with LDS models.
Relating switching LDS models to local linear approximations of non-linear low-rank RNNs.
papers.abstract: A large body of work has suggested that neural populations exhibit low-dimensional dynamics during behavior. However, there are a variety of different approaches for modeling low-dimensional neural population activity.
